answer.rationale:
Structural constraints do most of the work here before any memory is consulted. With 14 days to expiry, the line at 94% of committed volume, and zero buffer, any action that requires onboarding or qualification time is disqualified on delivery-risk grounds regardless of how favorable the record looks. That rules out switch_primary_vendor (memory_c2) and, for this cycle, add_second_source (memory_c3) — c3 is a genuinely good lesson but it was learned about a constrained component with lead time to absorb the change, not a primary contract expiring in two weeks against a full line. defer_decision (memory_c5) is explicitly disanalogous: c5 concerned a non-critical service that could continue month-to-month; this contract does not auto-renew, so deferring produces a supply cliff rather than budget flexibility. That leaves renew_incumbent or negotiate_terms, and negotiation strictly dominates plain renewal since it preserves the continuity benefit recorded in memory_c1 while still attacking the 18% mandate.

So I spend the single verification on the memory my chosen action actually rests on, not the most tempting alternative. memory_c4 is load-bearing: it claims benchmarking recovered 'real margin' on both price and payment terms, but 'real margin' is unquantified. If the original record shows something like 3-5%, negotiation alone cannot reach 18% and I need to tell finance now that the mandate requires scope or design change, not vendor pressure. If it shows double digits, the path is credible. Verifying memory_c2 would be verifying an option I have already excluded on timing grounds — and I note c2 is suspiciously silent on delivery performance, recording only unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy, which is exactly the omission that would matter and exactly why I am not betting the line on it.

Downstream value risk: pursuing 18% purely through price compression is where this goes wrong. memory_c6 says the multi-year commitment cut unit cost 'without narrowing the service scope,' which is a real signal but also a single observation — the same lever pulled harder can quietly trade away expediting rights, allocation priority, or quality inspection, and at 94% utilization I would not see the damage until a miss I cannot absorb. I therefore negotiate at standard scale with a moderate term rather than locking a maximal multi-year commitment, hold service scope and allocation priority as non-negotiable, and carry add_second_source forward as the top candidate for the next review once buffer exists. Uncertainty preserved: c4's magnitude is unknown until verified, c2's delivery record is unobserved rather than good, and the 18% target may simply not be reachable through sourcing alone.
